{{image-1}}

This past Friday, while you were likely asleep or binging Netflix from the comfort of your home, I was huddled outside of a closed mall, at 3 am, somewhat cold and starved, like some middle class Oliver Twist or a baby bird waiting to be fed from the gracious yet scarce mouth of Mother Capitalism. I’ve never camped out for anything before. As a teenager, I was into video games and shoes, both of which have seen their fair share of limited releases, but something about leaving the house before even the sun decided to wake up just to buy a product kept me away (or maybe it was the lack of a car…and a license). But here I was, participating in the biblical levels of greed that I laugh at in TikTok videos of grown men tackling each other for the chance to buy children’s trading cards.[^1] I didn’t know what to expect honestly. I figured I’d get there, sit down and read a book or something while I waited and emerge later with my product miserable but satisfied (for the moment). What I didn’t expect to encounter was a deeply human experience that I’ll cherish long after the phone is gone.

When I say that this was a deeply human experience, I mean that in the best and worst way. The morning started organized and respectful. Apparently, you’re not allowed on mall property until 7 am, so we made a neat line near the parking lot based on what time people arrived (some people were there as early as 1 am). We didn’t need to stay in line, no one was going to cut, we just put a backpack, a box, or a chair where our place in line was and got in our cars to stay warm. This state of affairs did not last long. One guy started walking toward the doors of the mall (I found out after asking him later that he was just looking for security) and groupthink quickly took over. Next thing I knew, we were all out of our cars, in the cold, waiting by the front door. There were arguments about places in line, who arrived when, etc. The security guard had to kick us off the property. Twice actually, because the same situation happened later closer to opening time once enough people arrived who weren’t part of the first wave. They did not listen to the security guard this time. The line outside the mall no longer mattered. When you arrived no longer mattered. Whoever made it inside to the Apple Store last was a rotten egg. By the time the security guard opened the doors, there was pushing, chaos, and a scene that looked like something out of the Walking Dead. This was the first time I’ve raced other human beings for anything tangible since elementary school.[^2] So there’s the wild stuff that happened. People being people, not trusting each other, insisting on their own way, fighting, allat. But aside from the crazy stuff, I also had a chance to connect with strangers in a way I normally don’t.

I’m embarrassed to say that upon reflection, I don’t remember the last time I spent real time in a conversation with strangers. I mean people who don’t come from anywhere in my social Venn diagram. Which is very different from strangers at work, church, or my neighborhood because we’re still, in someway, in each others orbit. These are people who I have never seen and likely will never see again. But when you’re standing out in the cold at 4 am, conversation with just about anyone sounds real good. And so I met people. I met a gay Episcopalian gymnast who spent most of the night beefing with a stereotypical older Mediterranean woman (their back-and-forth kept the otherwise quiet morning colorful). He initiated conversation with me while I sat cheeks on concrete with my laptop trying (in vain) to focus on finishing out a 15-page theology paper for class. We had some great conversations about faith, church hurt, and his work with kid athletes. I met his friend, a girl, whom I spoke with less, but I observed she has a gift for loving on people. Many times during the night she was the one breaking up arguments or taking someone who needed to cool off for a little walk in the night air. We also bonded over our love for the Canadian sweatwear brand Roots. I met an Amtrak IT engineer (he’s the guy who went to look for security). We were the most similar in temperament and so I think we gravitated toward sticking together while watching the chaos unfold. He also cooked me in Switch Sports bowling while we waited in line. I met a dude who got his master’s in computer science, but after not having much luck in the job market, he pivoted to running his own small business, which he still does now. I had the kinds of conversations usually reserved for friends with strangers and that was nice.

We joked with each other that we had become a little “Apple family”. Hanging out outside a closed mall for six hours will do that to you. And as each of us entered the pearly gates of the Apple Store to claim our prize, it felt like watching the credits for the final episode of your favorite sitcom. For a moment in the store, buying the phone didn’t seem so important anymore. I don’t think any of us were particularly interested in keeping contact afterward, I have a hard time keeping up with the friends I have as is. But still, I lingered for a bit while waiting for them to get theirs. Something I’ve learned is that most experiences last for a moment. We can try to replicate that experience: run the trip back, go back to that great restaurant, go on another date, but that’s always a different experience, a different moment. I’m learning to respect that each moment is different and to appreciate each moment for what it is. To look forward to the joys of the next moment, which will be different, rather than getting back what was. I guess lingering in the store was my way of trying to acknowledge that the moment was over and that I enjoyed it.

I don’t have a good close here. I kind of rambled in the last section, but that’s because it’s hard to take felt experience and distill it down into shareable words. When you experience something beautiful, you want to share it. That’s what humans do. Our joy is completed in a thing when we share it. So I guess this is just my way of doing that. For something more concrete, I was listening to an episode of the _Savy Psychologist_ by Dr. Judy Ho and she mentioned that having real conversations with strangers can alleviate loneliness, even for people who feel surrounded by friends and family.[^3] So maybe talk to the checkout person at Trader Joe’s more. There’s your lesson.

[^1]: [This](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ovqh7nEuzLI) is one of my favorite videos because one man, overwhelmed by his own greed, falls backwards and the other greed lords swoop down to pick him clean like vultures. It’s beautiful

[^2]: Of course, I was one of the first to make it over from our group because I run a seven minute mile. Turns out that didn’t matter though because they opened the other mall doors first and we were all late to the party.

[^3]: Episode [Link](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/why-do-i-feel-lonely-even-when-my-life-is-full/id803978236?i=1000789750358)
